Adults aged 18 or over can pay up to £20,000 into ISAs in the 2026/27 tax year, which runs from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027.

You can split that allowance between cash ISAs, stocks and shares ISAs, innovative finance ISAs and a Lifetime ISA. The Lifetime ISA has its own limit of £4,000. Any unused allowance does not carry forward.

Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

The ISA allowance for 2026/27 is £20,000 for adults aged 18 or over. The tax year runs from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027.

You can split the £20,000 between cash ISAs, stocks and shares ISAs, innovative finance ISAs and a Lifetime ISA. The Lifetime ISA has its own limit of £4,000. Unused allowance does not carry forward.

More detail is in the ISA guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

Our ISA guide says adults aged 18 or over can pay up to £20,000 into ISAs in the 2026/27 tax year. It also says a Lifetime ISA can be opened by anyone aged 18 to 39. It does not say whether someone under 18 can open an ISA with us, so I can't confirm whether your daughter can.

Please raise this with your adviser. The guide is here: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

You can pay up to £4,000 a year into a Lifetime ISA. That counts towards the £20,000 overall ISA allowance. The government adds a 25% bonus, worth up to £1,000 a year.

You must be aged 18 to 39 to open one. Withdrawals other than the permitted ones incur a 25% government charge. The permitted ones are:
- buying a first home costing £450,000 or less, once the account has been open for at least 12 months
- withdrawals from age 60
- withdrawals if you are terminally ill with less than 12 months to live

More detail is in the ISA guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

A Lifetime ISA can be opened by anyone aged 18 to 39.

Adults aged 18 or over can pay up to £20,000 into ISAs in the 2026/27 tax year, which runs from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. The allowance can be split between cash ISAs, stocks and shares ISAs, innovative finance ISAs and a Lifetime ISA, subject to the Lifetime ISA's own limit of £4,000.

Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

The ISA guide lists these changes from 6 April 2027:

- **Cash ISA cap:** Investors under 65 can pay up to £12,000 a tax year into cash ISAs. The overall £20,000 allowance is unchanged. The remainder can still go into stocks and shares or innovative finance ISAs. Investors aged 65 and over keep a £20,000 cash ISA limit.
- **Transfers:** You will no longer be able to transfer from stocks and shares or innovative finance ISAs into cash ISAs.
- **Interest charge:** A charge will apply to interest paid on cash held inside a stocks and shares or innovative finance ISA.
- **Existing money:** Money already in cash ISAs isn't affected by the cap.

Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

I can't say what you should do with your own ISAs. For that, please speak to an adviser.

The guide says investors aged 65 and over keep a £20,000 cash ISA limit. The £12,000 cash ISA cap applies to investors under the age of 65, from 6 April 2027. The guide doesn't mention any specific age other than those thresholds, so I can't confirm anything beyond that for your own circumstances.

The guide also says money already held in cash ISAs is not affected by the cap. For advice on your own situation, please raise it with your adviser.

Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

Under HM Revenue & Customs' guidelines, transfers between cash ISAs should take no longer than 15 working days. Other ISA transfers should take no longer than 30 calendar days. Re-registering holdings in specie can take longer if fund managers are slow to respond.

The new provider starts the transfer. Use their transfer process rather than withdrawing the money, so the ISA keeps its tax status. We don't charge for transfers in or out.

Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

Yes. Our stocks and shares ISA is flexible. You can replace money you withdraw in the same tax year without using more of your allowance.

The documents don't say anything more, such as whether any conditions apply. For anything specific to your circumstances, please raise it with your adviser. More detail is at https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

A surviving spouse or civil partner is entitled to an additional permitted subscription equal to the value of the deceased's ISAs, in addition to their own allowance, whether or not they inherit the investments themselves.

The documents also say the ISA continues to be tax-free as a continuing account of a deceased investor for up to three years while the estate is administered. They do not say how this would apply in your circumstances, so please raise that with your adviser.

The pension annual allowance is £60,000. If the total paid into your pensions in a tax year goes over it, an annual allowance charge is normally due. The total includes employer contributions and the value of any defined benefit accrual.

- For high earners, the allowance tapers down to a minimum of £10,000.
- You can carry forward unused allowance from the previous three tax years. This only applies if you were a member of a registered pension scheme in those years.
- Once you have taken taxable income flexibly from a defined contribution pension, the money purchase annual allowance of £10,000 applies to further defined contribution contributions.

More detail is in the pensions guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/pensions/

I can't tell you how this applies to your own situation. For that, please ask an adviser.

Once you have taken taxable income flexibly from a defined contribution pension, the money purchase annual allowance of £10,000 applies to further defined contribution contributions.

The documents don't say anything more on whether you can pay in or how this applies to you. Please raise that with your adviser.

Normally, you can take up to 25% of a pension tax free. This is subject to the lump sum allowance of £268,275 across all your pensions. Lump sums above that allowance are taxed at your marginal rate.

I can't advise on how much you should take or when. If you want advice on that, I can pass you to an adviser. More detail is at https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/pensions/

You can draw from a defined contribution pension from age 55, rising to 57 from 6 April 2028. The options are flexi-access drawdown, buying an annuity, taking lump sums, or a combination. Each has different tax consequences.

When you apply to access a pension, we will refer you to Pension Wise and offer to book a free guidance appointment for you, as the rules require, unless you have already had one or have received regulated advice.

Yes. If the transfer value is more than £30,000, the law requires you to take appropriate independent advice before the transfer can proceed. The advice must come from a firm with Financial Conduct Authority permission to advise on pension transfers. Fernhill Wealth holds that permission.

The Financial Conduct Authority expects advisers to start from the assumption that a transfer won't be suitable. Fernhill recommends one only where it can show the transfer is clearly in your interest. The documents don't say what applies at £30,000 or below. If that's your situation, please raise it with your adviser.

Based on our pensions guide:

From 6 April 2027, most unused pension funds and death benefits will be included in the value of your estate for inheritance tax. Benefits passing to a spouse or civil partner, or to a registered charity, remain exempt. Dependants' scheme pensions and death-in-service benefits are outside the new rules.

Income tax is separate. If you die before 75, benefits are normally paid free of income tax, within the lump sum and death benefit allowance of £1,073,100. If you die at or after 75, the recipient pays income tax at their marginal rate.

The documents don't say how this applies to your own circumstances. Please raise that with your adviser. Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/pensions/

Your own contributions receive tax relief up to 100% of your relevant UK earnings in the tax year, or £3,600 gross if your earnings are lower. Basic-rate relief is added to the pension automatically.

The guide doesn't say what applies if you have no earnings at all, so I can't confirm that for you. Please raise it with your adviser. Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/pensions/

Yes. Our pensions guide says unused annual allowance from the previous three tax years can be carried forward, provided you were a member of a registered pension scheme in those years.

The annual allowance is £60,000. For high earners it tapers down to a minimum of £10,000. The guide doesn't say how much you personally could carry forward. Please ask your adviser about that. More detail is at https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/pensions/

The annual exempt amount for capital gains tax is £3,000. It applies to gains on investments sold in a general investment account. Gains above that on shares and funds are taxed at 18% or 24%, depending on your total taxable income.

You can set losses against gains in the same year. You can also carry them forward if you report them to HMRC. Gains within an ISA or pension are free of UK capital gains tax. More detail is at https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/tax/

For investments held outside an ISA or pension in the 2026/27 tax year:

- Dividends are tax-free within the dividend allowance of £500 a year.
- Above the allowance, dividends are taxed at 10.75% for basic-rate taxpayers, 35.75% for higher-rate taxpayers and 39.35% for additional-rate taxpayers.

This is general information, not personal advice. Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/tax/
